title: A Modest Moral Realism
abstract: This project emerged from my desire to explore the nature of moral truth as it compares to other sorts of truth, which is a critical topic in moral philosophy. If we accept science as eminently “real,” how “real” is morality? I approached this question by diving into foundational scholarship in the philosophy of science and meta-ethics, particularly from Kant, Hume, Richard Boyd, Arthur Fine, Bernard Williams, and Hilary Putnam. Through my reading, I came to view scientific reality as a matter of humanity’s observation. That which is “scientifically real” is that which we happen to receive through our physical senses. We cannot claim any deeper ontology for physical reality than that we all experience it. Accordingly, it seemed to me that morality would maintain a similar level of reality to physicality if it achieved a similar experiential consensus. On analysis, it appeared that such experiential consensus is roughly met by morality, with some important caveats. I then composed a paper arguing for each of these findings. By taking science and morality from the heavens and placing them on the ground, my paper defends moral truth as an empirical discovery, just like scientific truth. The significance of my paper is its commentary on how we ought to view moral thought. I argue that if scientific advancement represents progress towards truth, moral development does as well. If I am right, morality deserves a seat directly next to science at the table of empirical human knowledge.
